b2-137.title: Dogs in the Park
b2-137.story: On Saturday, Anna and Max took Lisa's dogs to the park by the river. Lisa has a [[golden retriever]] called Sunny and a tiny [[corgi]] called Biscuit. Sunny jumped straight into the water, like every [[retriever]] does when it sees a lake. Biscuit tried to follow, but his short legs only got him as far as the mud. At the gate, they met a man with a black [[labrador]] who recommended a café nearby. "It's completely [[dog friendly]]," he said. "They even give dogs free water." Unfortunately, the café was not as [[pet-friendly]] as he had promised, and the waiter sighed when he saw the muddy little dog. In the end, they drank their coffee outside while two wet, happy dogs slept under the table.

b2-138.title: A Day on Safari
b2-138.story: For Taras's birthday, the whole family spent a day at a [[safari park]] outside the city. First they took a [[jeep safari]], and a guide drove them slowly past giraffes and sleeping lions. In the tropical house, a [[toucan]] with a bright orange beak watched them from a branch. Taras was disappointed that the [[anaconda]] was hiding under a rock and refused to move. Outside, an [[emu]] ran along the fence next to their car, as if it wanted to race them. At the petting area, a fluffy [[alpaca]] tried to eat Mama's hat. Near the exit stood a young [[sequoia]], which the guide said could live for three thousand years. They finished the day by a small [[cascade]] of water, where Taras announced that he wanted to become a zookeeper.

b2-139.title: Three Generations Talk
b2-139.story: For a school project, Anna interviewed three generations of her family about their lives. Her grandfather, a [[baby boomer]] born in 1950, said nobody on his street had a phone when he was a boy. Her dad, a typical [[millennial]], laughed and said he couldn't imagine life without Wi-Fi. Grandpa, a real [[extrovert]], told stories for an hour, although his [[pessimism]] about modern technology made Dad roll his eyes. "We were [[middle class]], but we worked hard for everything we had," Grandpa explained. When Anna asked about his greatest [[ideal]], he said it had always been helping other people. That's why he still works as a [[volunteer]], visiting every [[veteran]] in the local hospital once a week. They finished the interview at the [[barbershop]], where Grandpa and Dad asked for exactly the same haircut. Anna decided the generations weren't so different after all.

b2-140.title: A Summer at the Border
b2-140.story: Last summer, Max's sister Sofia worked as an interpreter at a port in a town on the US–Mexico border. Every morning she walked past the [[dock]] where an enormous [[tanker]] was being repaired. One of the workers was an [[immigrant]] from Ukraine who had moved there twenty years earlier. He paid for their tacos in [[pesos|peso]] and joked that he still counted prices in hryvnias. He even showed her an old Soviet [[ruble]] from his grandfather's coin collection. Most of Sofia's work, though, was at the [[checkpoint]], where every [[migrant]] had to show documents to the officers. One young woman was in tears because she had lost her [[green card]] somewhere on the journey. Sofia helped her fill in the forms, and an hour later an officer found the card in the lost-and-found box. That evening, the port workers were arguing about a new [[tariff]] on imported steel, but Sofia was simply happy about her small success.

b2-141.title: People at the Meetup
b2-141.story: Ira invited Anna to a small [[meetup]] for young photographers in a café downtown. Anna, a shy [[introvert]], almost stayed home, but Ira refused to go alone. The organizer turned out to be a [[life coach]] who believed everyone should step out of their comfort zone. She asked each person to describe themselves in one word. A boy in the corner called himself a [[pessimist]] because he was sure his photos were terrible. Ira, who had been a [[tomboy]] as a kid and still climbed trees for good shots, chose the word "brave." Anna admitted she was a [[perfectionist]] who deleted ninety percent of her pictures. By the end of the evening, the gloomy boy had shown everyone a beautiful photo, and Anna had promised to keep her pictures for once.

b2-142.title: How Our Street Changed
b2-142.story: For the school newspaper, Anna wrote an article about how her street in Kyiv had changed over ten years. The old bakery had become a [[tattoo salon]], and the shoe repair shop next to it was now a [[sex shop]] with dark windows. Grandma still complained about the nightclub across the road that had once advertised a [[striptease]] show. Anna also interviewed Mr. Koval, an [[emigrant]] who had come back from Canada after twenty years abroad. He said the biggest change he noticed was how open young people had become. His nephew, who is [[bisexual]], had recently marched in the city's [[gay pride]] parade without hiding it from anyone. At the same time, Mr. Koval warned that some things had gotten worse, because a [[scammer]] had just called him pretending to be from his bank. When a boy on the newspaper team said the article was "too serious for a girl to write," Anna told him not to be a [[sexist]]. The editor agreed with her and put the article on the front page.

b2-143.title: Trouble in Town
b2-143.story: Last week, someone sprayed paint all over the youth center where Max's sister Sofia volunteers. The police called it [[vandalism]], and the neighbors immediately blamed a local [[hooligan]] named Den. Sofia didn't believe it, because Den came to the center every day to play chess. He had grown up in a district that people unfairly called a [[ghetto]]. Sofia also knew that he had left home after years of [[abuse]] and worked hard to stay out of trouble. Two days later, a group of older teenagers was caught [[shoplifting]] at the mall, with the same paint still in their bags. Their leader had also been running an online [[scam]], selling fake concert tickets to younger kids. The neighbors apologized to Den, and that weekend he helped Sofia repaint the wall.

b2-144.title: Grandpa's Gangster Movie
b2-144.story: On Friday night, Grandpa made everyone watch his favorite black-and-white movie about the [[mafia]] in 1930s Chicago. The main character was a charming [[gangster]] who always had a perfect [[alibi]] for every crime. In the first scene, he hid a small [[pistol]] inside his hat, which Taras thought was the coolest thing ever. Later, an angry farmer chased the gang away from his barn with a [[shotgun]], and even Grandma laughed. The hero was an honest [[constable]] from London who carried an old [[revolver]] but never fired it. When a body turned up in the city [[morgue]], the newspapers blamed a [[maniac]], but the detective suspected the gang's boss. The boss was a cold [[sadist]] who enjoyed frightening his own men, and in the end they were the ones who betrayed him. Taras fell asleep before the ending, so Grandpa had to tell him the whole plot again at breakfast.
